summary: Cadillac's first Australian model has been updated for MY27 with a smaller 92kWh pack, 503km WLTP range and slower 130kW DC charging, still at the $90,000 before on-road costs that a permanent $32,000 cut set, which keeps the Sport (now the only regular grade, the Luxury having been dropped) under the fuel-efficient LCT threshold; the new 459kW Lyriq-V adds a $99,000 performance grade above it, with deliveries due from late in the first quarter of 2027. Reviewers agree on the hushed ride and distinctive styling but split on the cabin: CarExpert finds it comfortable and luxurious, while Chasing Cars judges the materials and rear seat not good enough at any price. The unresolved risks are a thin retail network, no Australian tow rating, and resale values re-based by the price cut.
pros: The Sport's $90,000 before on-road costs sits under the $91,661 fuel-efficient LCT threshold, so it qualifies for the FBT exemption on a novated lease; the $99,000 Lyriq-V does not.
503km WLTP range for the Sport (471km for the Lyriq-V) and a 22.1kW three-phase AC onboard charger, double the 11kW most rivals fit, which Cadillac rates at up to 105km of range per hour of charging.

The MY27 update adds lane centring and traffic sign recognition, fixing the earlier car's adaptive cruise that could not steer, and upgrades the AKG Studio audio from 19 to 23 speakers with Dolby Atmos.
Five-year unlimited-kilometre warranty, an eight-year/160,000km battery warranty and five years of premium roadside assistance, with 24-month/24,000km service intervals.
The Lyriq-V's 459kW/880Nm and claimed 3.6-second 0-100km/h make it the quickest Cadillac yet for $9,000 more than the Sport, and CarExpert calls its V-Mode genuinely more engaging to drive.
cons: The MY27 range is a step back on paper: the pack shrinks from 102kWh to 92kWh, WLTP range falls from 530km to 503km, and peak DC charging drops from 190kW to 130kW, which CarExpert says leaves range and charging behind rivals.
Not rated to tow anything in Australia, where a Kia EV9 pulls 2,500kg braked and a Zeekr 7X 2,000kg.

A thin network: Cadillac's own outlets are the Rosebery Experience Centre in Sydney, a Port Melbourne test-drive venue and Auckland, with dealer partners promised but unnamed as of CarExpert's April 2026 report, so servicing can mean a long trip.
The $32,000 cut re-based every early Lyriq sold at $117,000 to $124,000, Cadillac does not report sales to VFACTS, and there is no local residual data to argue with.

Chasing Cars rates the rear seat's short, flat cushion and intrusive ISOFIX panel as genuinely uncomfortable and the cabin materials well below expectation, and CarExpert heard squeaks and creaks in the Lyriq-V; MY27 also loses the two front knee airbags.
